'''''Iris fulva''''', also known as '''copper iris''' or '''red flag''', is a species in the genus ''[[Iris (plant)|Iris]]'', it is also in the subgenus ''[[Iris subg. Limniris|Limniris]]'' and in the series ''[[Louisiana iris|Hexagonae]]''. It is a [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], endemic to the southern and central United States. It has copper-red to deep red flowers and bright green leaves.

==Description==
''Iris fulva'' has slender greenish-brown rhizome (or occasionally red,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=Bergmann>{{cite web |first=Karel |last=Bergmann  |title=IRIS FULVA Ker Gawl. – Copper Iris |date=24 April 2014 |url=http://botany.cz/en/iris-fulva/ |publisher= botany.cz |access-date=5 December 2014}}</ref>) that has the (ring-like) scars of old leaves (from previous seasons).<ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=ohio>{{cite journal |last=Waller |first=Adolph E. |title=The Native Iris of Ohio and Bordering Territory |date=January 1931 |journal=Ohio Journal of Science |volume=31 |issue=1 |publisher=The Ohio State University |hdl=1811/2488 }}</ref> They are approximately 1.5–2 cm in diameter,<ref name=efloras>{{cite web |title=Flora of North America, ''Iris fulva''|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101701 |publisher=efloras.org |access-date=2 December 2014}}</ref> shallow rooted with fibrous roots underneath and can form many branches.<ref name=illnois/><ref name=fsfed>{{cite web |title=Iris fulva |url=http://www.fs.fed.us/wildflowers/beauty/iris/louisiana/iris_fulva.shtml |publisher=fs.fed.us |access-date=2 December 2014}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=efloras/>--> Which eventually spread out to create large clumps around 1–2 feet wide.<ref name=tina/><ref name=award/><ref name=irfu/><!-- also <ref name=fsfed/><ref name=copperiris/>-->

It grows new leaves early in the autumn, which can pass through the winter into the spring. This means that the plant is generally only leafless around August time.<ref name=handbook/> The leaves are bright green, blade-like (meaning long and narrow), lightly ribbed (parallel to the stem) and rise from the base of the plant but then arch away from the stem.<ref name=illnois/><ref name=irfu/><ref name=copperiris>{{cite web |title=Copper Iris |url=http://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/copper-iris |publisher=mdc.mo.gov |access-date=5 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150729043831/http://mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/copper-iris |archive-date=29 July 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=fsfed/>--> They can measure between {{convert|60|–|100|cm|ftin|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=cassidy/> and between 1–2 cm (½ to 1 inch) wide.<ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=award/><ref name=Nash/><!-- also <ref name=illnois/>--> It was noted by [[William Rickatson Dykes|Dykes]], that when held up the light, the leaves have black dots, which are similar to water-irises leaves.<ref name=handbook/> Some leaves emerge along the flower stem (which is known as cauline in botany terms).<ref name=efloras/><ref name=illnois/>

The flower stem is generally straight with one or two branches (or joints), and can reach up to a height of between {{convert|45|–|80|cm|in|abbr=on}}. tall.<ref name=tina/><ref name=cassidy>{{cite book |last1=Cassidy |first1=George E.| last2=Linnegar | first2=Sidney | date=1987 |edition=Revised  |title= Growing Irises |location=Bromley |publisher=Christopher Helm | isbn=0-88192-089-4}}</ref><ref name="southern">Neil G. Odenwald and James R. Turner {{Google books|Identification, Selection, and Use of Southern Plants: For Landscape Design|S__s1QADDJoC|page=316}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=stebbings/><ref name=RHS/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=pacific/><ref name=american/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=ohio/><ref name=copperiris/><ref name=irfu/>--> The stem is mid-green in colour, with 1–3 alternate leaves rising along the stem, that are very similar (but smaller) to the basal leaves.<ref name=ohio/><ref name=illnois/>

It normally flowers between spring and early summer,<ref name=tina/> between April and June,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=copperiris/> with one or two flowers per axil of each alternate leaf along the stem.<ref name=cassidy/><ref name=american/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=handbook/><ref name=fsfed/><ref name=illnois/><ref name=award/>--> There can be as many as 4–6 (occasionally more) flowers per stem.<ref name=RHS/> In Australia and New Zealand, they bloom between September and November.<ref name=Nash/> The blooming period lasts for about 3 weeks. Although the individual flowers are fairly short-lived (lasting for about 1–4 days).<ref name=illnois/><ref name=Nash/>

[[File:Iris fulva 4.JPG|thumb|left|Copper iris in bloom, close-up]]
The flowers are slightly fragrant,<ref name=illnois/> and come in a range of shades of red, from copper-red (reddish orange to brownish orange),<ref name=pacific/><ref name=RHS/><ref name=keys>{{cite web |first=Daniel B. |last=Ward |title=KEYS TO THE FLORA OF FLORIDA – 28, IRIS (IRIDACEAE) | url=http://www.phytologia.org/uploads/2/3/4/2/23422706/932231-240wardirisesflorida.pdf | publisher=Phytologia (Department of Botany, University of Florida) | date=August 2011 }}</ref><!-- also <ref name=fsfed/><ref name=illnois/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=Nash/>--> to brick-red,<ref name=irfu/><ref name=stebbings/><ref name=arkansas>{{cite book|first=Edwin B.|last=Smith|title=Keys to the Flora of Arkansas|url={{Google books|id=4HMxfXJYyzkC|page=327|plainurl=yes}}|page=327|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024|publisher=University of Arkansas Press|year=1994|isbn=1-55728-312-5}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=fsfed/>--> to rust-red,<ref name=Nash/><ref name=southern/> to deep red,<ref name=american/> and bronze.<ref name=tina/><ref name=Nash/><ref name=keys/> Occasionally there are yellow flowered forms.<ref name=tina/><ref name=cassidy/><ref name=pacific/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=fsfed/><ref name=illnois/>--> Unlike many other irises, the flower on the falls and standards are the same colour.<ref name=handbook/>

It has a 2–2.5 cm perianth tube.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=award/>

''Iris fulva'' is unusual, as its six-petalled flowers all droop away from the middle section.<ref name=irfu/><ref name=american/><ref name=southern/><!-- also <ref name=handbook/><ref name=fsfed/><ref name=illnois/><ref name=copperiris/>--> The flowers are wide spread, have three drooping falls (or sepals),<ref name=ohio/><ref name=copperiris/> which are {{convert|1|-|1.25|in|cm|abbr=on}} wide and {{convert|2.25|-|2.5|in|cm|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=award/><ref name=Nash/><ref name=southern/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=illnois/>--> and three drooping standards (or petals),<ref name=ohio/><ref name=copperiris/><ref name=cassidy/> which are 4.5 cm long and {{convert|5|–|7|cm|in|abbr=on}} across.<ref name=award/><ref name=american/><ref name=RHS/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=illnois/>--> The base of each flower is tubular and has a yellowish centre.<ref name=illnois/><ref name=copperiris/>

The flower has short styles (female parts) which are about 2 cm long.<ref name=ohio/><ref name=american/> Inside the flower, the stigma has two small pointed teeth (or lobes).<ref name=efloras/> The filaments (stalks holding the anther) are yellow, the anthers are cream, reaching the stigma, the pollen is cream.<ref name=ohio/>

''[[Iris brevicaulis]]'' and ''Iris fulva'' share very similar looking seed-pods (capsules) and seeds.<ref name=handbook/>
The green capsules are six-angled (hexagonal in cross-section),<ref name=keys/><ref name=arkansas/> elliptical to oval (in shape) measuring between {{convert|4.5|–|8|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|2.5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=ohio/><ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=american/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=illnois/>--> The seeds are stored in two rows within the capsules.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=illnois/> The seeds are flat and irregular (in shape), measuring 10-15mm wide.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=ohio/> Like other Louisiana irises they are covered in a cork-like substance, which allows them to float on the water (within the swamp habitats) to new locations.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=ohio/><ref name=illnois/>

===Genetics===
As most irises are [[diploid]], they have two sets of [[chromosomes]]. This fact can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book | first= Claire | last=Austin | title= Irises: A Gardener's Encyclopedia | publisher= Timber Press, Incorporated | isbn = 978-0881927306 | year = 2005 | ol = OL8176432M }}</ref>
It has a chromosome count: 2n=42,<ref name=efloras/><ref name=signa/><ref name=pacific>{{cite web| title=Iris summary |date=14 April 2014 |url=http://www.pacificbulbsociety.org/pbswiki/files/Iris/Iris_Summary.pdf |publisher=pacificbulbsociety.org |access-date=28 November 2014}}</ref> It has been counted several times. 2n=42, differing from some other Louisiana iris species, so hybrids from crossing with those other species should have an odd number of chromosomes, for example, if an iris with 44 is crossed with this species, the hybrids should have 43 chromosomes. Simonet 1932, 2n=42-Riley 1942; 2n=42 by [[Lowell Fitz Randolph|Randolph]] & Mitra 1961; 2n-42, Randolph, 1966.<ref name=american/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Iris fulva 1.jpg|thumb|Iris fulva]]
It has the common name of 'Copper Iris'.<ref name=tina>{{cite book|first=Tina M.|last=Samuels|title=A Georgia Native Plant Guide|url={{Google books|id=or8aLEAqHiIC|page=45|plainurl=yes}}|page=45|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024|publisher=Mercer University Press|year=2005|isbn=0-86554-878-1|chapter=Georgia Native Flowers}}</ref><ref name=signa>{{cite web |first=D. |last=Kramb |date=18 September 2004 |title=Iris fulva |url=http://www.signa.org/index.pl?Iris-fulva |publisher=signa.org (Species Iris Group of North America) |access-date=5 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | accessdate=29 April 2015}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=fsfed/><ref name=copperiris/>-->

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] 'Fulva' comes from the [[Latin]] for 'tawny-orange'.<ref>{{cite book |last=Stearn |first=William |year=1972 |title=A Gardenerer's Dictionary of Plant Names |location=London |publisher=Cassell |page=211 |isbn=0304937215 }}</ref>

It was first found and collected on the banks of the [[Mississippi River]] near [[New Orleans]] in 1811.<ref name=handbook>{{cite web |first=William |last=Dykes |title=Handbook of Garden Irises |year=2009 |url=http://www.beardlessiris.org/reviews/handbook%20of%20garden%20irises%20-%20dykes.pdf |publisher=beardlessiris.org (The Group for Beardless Irises) |access-date=2 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=Lucille>{{cite book|first=Lucille|last=Parker|title=Southern Wildflowers|url={{Google books|id=13iVq6l1WHgC|plainurl=yes}}|publisher=Pelican Publishing Company|year=1999|orig-date=Originally published 1981|isbn=1-56554-419-6|page=18|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024}}</ref>

It was then first published and described by [[John Bellenden Ker Gawler]] in the [[Botanical Magazine]] Issue 36 of 1812.<ref name=grin/><ref>{{cite web |title=Iridaceae Iris fulva Ker Gawl. |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=438620-1 |publisher=ipni.org ([[International Plant Names Index]]) |access-date=2 December 2014}}</ref>
It was later published in '[[Addisonia (journal)|Addisonia]]' Issue 12 in March 1927 with colour illustrations.<ref name=american>{{cite web |title=(SPEC) Iris fulva Ker-Gawl  |date=20 October 2014 |first=Terry |last=Laurin  |url=http://wiki.irises.org/bin/view/Spec/SpecFulva |publisher=wiki.irises.org (American Iris Society) |access-date=2 December 2014}}</ref>

[[John James Audubon]] illustrated a pair of Northern Parulas in ''[[Birds of America (book)|Birds of America]]'', (published, London 1827–38), Plate 15 entitled "Blue Yellow-backed Warbler – ''Sylvia americana''". The birds are shown perched on a Louisiana Flag (''Iris fulva'') painted by his assistant [[Joseph Mason (artist)|Joseph Mason]] to which Audubon added the two birds in 1821. This led to a group of Irises in Louisiana known as the "[[Louisiana Irises]]".<ref name=zyco>{{cite web |first=Tom W. |last=Dillard |title=FROM NEW ORLEANS TO NEW ZEALAND, History and Development of The Louisiana Irises |url=http://zydecoirises.com/Species/Species.htm |publisher=zydecoirises.com |access-date=28 November 2014}}</ref><ref name=Seidenberg>{{cite book|first=Charlotte|last=Seidenberg|title=The New Orleans Garden: Gardening in the Gulf South|url={{Google books|id=11p5PhNOQ3UC|page=223|plainurl=yes}}|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024|pages=223–224|isbn=0-87805-637-8|publisher=University Press of Mississippi|orig-date=Originally published 1990 by Silkmont & Count|year=1993}}</ref>

It was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 4 April 2003, and then updated on 1 December 2004.<ref name=grin/> ''Iris fulva'' is also an accepted name by the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]] and it has been awarded with the [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name=award>{{cite web |title=Search for AGM plants |url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/agm/Award3.asp?ID=58091  |publisher=rhs.org.uk |access-date=4 December 2014}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Caddo parish iris fulva.jpg|thumb|''Iris fulva'' in flower]]
It is [[native plant|native]] to North America.<ref name=grin/>

===Range===
''Iris fulva'' comes from the southern United States, including [[Arkansas]],<ref name=arkansas/><ref name=grin/> [[Illinois]],<ref name=illnois/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=grin/><!-- also <ref name=Bergmann/>--> (in the LaRue swamp on the [[Big Muddy River]]<ref>{{cite book|first=Robert H.|last=Mohlenbrock|title=This Land|url={{Google books|id=gupOE0x1BKYC|page=74|plainurl=yes}}|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024|pages=73–75|isbn=0-520-23984-9|publisher=University of California Press|year=2006}}</ref>), [[Kentucky]],<ref name=fsfed/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=grin/> Louisiana,<ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=grin/> (in the Mississippi valley,<ref name=cassidy/><ref name=pacific/>) [[Mississippi]], (along the banks of the Mississippi River, rarer on the eastern side),<ref name=Bergmann/><ref name=ClaireAustin/><ref name=grin/> [[Missouri]],<ref name=copperiris/><ref name=grin/> [[Ohio]], ([[Champaign County, Ohio|Champaign County]], [[Clark County, Ohio|Clark County]],<ref name=ohio/>), [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]],<ref name=tina/><ref name=ClaireAustin/> [[Florida]] (only found rarely in [[Santa Rosa County, Florida|Santa Rosa County]],<ref name=keys/>) and Tennessee.<ref name=fsfed/><ref name=irfu/><ref name=grin/><!-- also <ref name=efloras/>-->

===Habitat===
[[File:Iris fulva in habitat.jpg|thumb|''Iris fulva'' in habitat]]
''Iris fulva'' is found in freshwater, in marshes, stream banks, field or roadside ditches,<ref name=southern/> in drainage canals, swamps,<ref name=keys/> and wet pastures.<ref name=irfu/><ref name=Lucille/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Taylor |first1=Sunni J. |last2= Willard |first2=Rees W. |first3=Joshua P. |last3=Shaw  |first4=Mary C. |last4= Dobson |first5=Noland H. |last5=Martin |date=13 May 2011 |title=Differential response of the homoploid hybrid species ''Iris nelsonii'' (Iridaceae) and its progenitors to abiotic habitat conditions |journal=American Journal of Botany |publisher=Department of Biology, Texas State University–San Marcos |doi=10.3732/ajb.1100012 |volume=98 |issue=8 |pages=1309–1316 |pmid=21821591 |bibcode=2011AmJB...98.1309T }}</ref><!-- also <ref name=efloras/><ref name=illnois/><ref name=copperiris/>--> It is normally found in water up to {{convert|6|in|cm}} deep.<ref name=illnois/><ref name=Nash/>

==Conservation==
''Iris fulva'' is listed as 'endangered' in the states of Kentucky and Tennessee,<ref name=Bergmann/> and listed as 'threatened' in Illinois.<ref name=illnois/>

This is due to the loss of habitat. Which are under threats from dredging operations, also swamps that are being drained and 'toxic' farm herbicides running into ditches and streams.<ref name=copperiris/>

==Cultivation==
[[File:Iris Fulva.jpg|thumb|Close-up image of Iris fulva flower]]
The Louisiana irises generally all have similar cultivation requirements. They need full sunlight (minimum of six hours during summer), moist, acidic soils (pH level of 6.5) with a high organic and high fertility content.<ref name=illnois>{{cite web |title=Copper Iris |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/wetland/plants/copper_iris.html |publisher=illinoiswildflowers.info |access-date=5 December 2014}}</ref><ref name=Nash>Helen Nash {{Google books|Complete Guide to Water Garden Plants|ssKzSCtgyZ8C|pages=187–191}}</ref><ref name=Gill>{{cite web |first1=Dan |last1=Gill |first2=Allen |last2=Owings |title=Louisiana Iris |year=1969 |publisher=Louisiana State University |url=http://www.lsuagcenter.com/NR/rdonlyres/02E30CFB-734D-40A2-901067D23EBFB26A/38089/pub1969LAIrisFORWEB2.pdf |access-date=7 December 2014 }}{{Dead link|date=January 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><!-- also <ref name=signa/>-->

For best flowering, moisture is essential during late autumn, winter and spring times (October to May), when the plant starts to grow new leaves.<ref name=american/><ref name="southern"/> They can be given a light feed between autumn and spring, if needed.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=Gill/>

It is estimated to be [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] to between [[USDA]] Zones 3 to 10.<ref name=illnois/><ref name=signa/>

It can tolerate frost but will flower poorly in areas with cool summers.<ref name=Gill/><ref name=Australia/>

It can be grown in southern UK, in damp or wet soils.<ref name=stebbings>{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |year=1997|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb |url-access=registration |location=Newton Abbot |publisher=David and Charles |page=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/54 54] |isbn=0715305395 }}</ref><ref name=RHS>{{cite book|editor=Christopher Bricknell | title=Gardeners' Encyclopedia of Plants and Flowers| year=1989 |edition=1994) |page=522 |publisher=Dorling Kindersley| isbn=978-0751301472 }}</ref>
They can be grown in most of the United States, New Zealand and Australia.<ref name=Nash/>
They can be used planted by the edges of ponds and pools or they can be planted in the water.<ref name=tina/> But they need the rhizomes to be pinned into the ground to stop them floating away.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=southern/> Also the rhizomes must be covered in gravel to stop fish disturbing the roots.<ref name=Nash/> They can also be planted in streams, but not heavy flowing rivers.<ref name=Nash/> It can tolerate pools up to 6 inches deep.<ref name=illnois/>

They also can be grown in containers (even in the water or bog garden) but they must be re-potted and divided every year.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=Gill/>

If using a fertilizer, sprinkle around the plant in late January or February, before the plant is in flower.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=southern/><ref name=Gill/>

New plantings need to be mulched to prevent sun-scalding.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=Gill/> Plantings in the water do not need mulching and tend to grow quicker than others.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=Gill/>

===Propagation===
Propagation is best carried out by [[Division (horticulture)|division]] of the rhizomes.<ref name=southern/><ref name=Gill/><ref name=Australia>{{cite book|first=Nick|last=Romanowski|title=Water Garden Plants & Animals: The Complete Guide for All Australia|publisher=University of New South Wales Press|url={{Google books|id=gQsVgaxl-9kC|page=43|plainurl=yes}}|isbn=0-86840-418-7|via=Google Books|access-date=11 November 2024|pages=43–44|year=2000}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Dan |last=Gill |title=Get It Growing: It's Time To Divide Louisiana Irises, Get It Growing News |date=9 August 2006 |url=http://www.lsuagcenter.com/news_archive/2006/september/get_it_growing/Get+It+Growing+Its+Time+To+Divide+Louisiana+Irises.htm |publisher=lsuagcenter.com |access-date=8 December 2014 |archive-date=13 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141213204235/http://www.lsuagcenter.com/news_archive/2006/september/get_it_growing/Get+It+Growing+Its+Time+To+Divide+Louisiana+Irises.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><!-- also <ref name=Nash/>-->
Which is best carried out in late summer, when the plants are dormant. The ground must be prepared pre-planting, with the addition of a generous amount of organic matter and the soils dug to about 6 inches deep (to allow for new root growth). Plants require dividing every 3–4 years to promote good flowering. They can combine with other plants but tend to 'move' to suitable positions.<ref name=Nash/><ref name=southern/><ref name=Gill/>

The iris seed is not hard to raise but a very slow process.<ref name=Australia/> It can take many months to germinate (between 3–12 months) with a 50% germination average.<ref name=Nash/> They then can take 3–5 years before reaching flowering stage.<ref name=Australia/>

Seeds should be harvested from the plant after flowering but they must be from mature seed pods. They then should be stored in paper bags, as seed stored in glass containers often goes mouldy.<ref name=Nash/>

===Pollination===
''Iris fulva'' (like ''[[Iris brevicaulis]]'') is primary pollinated by hummingbirds looking for nectar,<ref name=irfu>{{cite web |title=Iris fulva |url=http://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=IRFU |publisher=wildflower.org |access-date=5 December 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Sunni J. |last1=Taylor |first2=Kendall J. |last2=AuBuchon |first3=Noland H. |last3=Martin |title=Identification of Floral Visitors of Iris nelsonii |url=http://www.eaglehill.us/SENAonline/articles/SENA-11-1/22-Taylor.shtml |journal=Notes of the Southeastern Naturalist |volume=11  |issue=1 |year=2012 |access-date=2 December 2014 |doi=10.1656/058.011.0114 |pages=141–144|s2cid=86326602 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Crespo |first1=Manuel B. |last2= Alonso |first2=Mª Angeles |first3=Mario |last3=Martínez-Azorín |first4= Alicia |last4=Vicente |first5=José Luis |last5=Villar |first6=Mathieu |last6= Chambouleyron  |year=2014 |title=New data on the recently described Xiphion heracleanum (Iridaceae), endemic to Morocco |journal=Phytotaxa |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.162.1.3 |volume=162 |issue=1 |pages=31|bibcode=2014Phytx.162...31C |s2cid=85821417 }}</ref> mainly the [[ruby-throated hummingbird]] (''Archilochus colubris'').<ref name=illnois/> It also attracts butterflies.<ref name=copperiris/><ref name=transmission>{{cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Shunxue |last2=Okashah |first2=Rebecca A |first3=Steven J |last3=Knapp |first4=Michael L |last4=Arnold |first5=Noland H |last5=Martin |year=2010 |title=Transmission ratio distortion results in asymmetric introgression in Louisiana Iris |url= |journal=BMC Plant Biology |publisher=Bio Med Central |volume=10 |issue=48  |pages=48 |doi=10.1186/1471-2229-10-48|pmid=20298609 |pmc=2923522 |bibcode=2010BMCPB..10...48T |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Hybrids and cultivars===
''Iris fulva'' can easily hybridize with other Louisiana irises to create new variants. The first was 'Iris fulvala' a hybrid [[William Rickatson Dykes|Dykes]] raised as a cross between ''Iris fulva'' and ''Iris brevicaulis''. 
It produced two forms, both with rich velvety falls, one a red-purple form and the other was a bluer shade.<ref name=efloras/><ref name=cassidy/> The name was composed of ''Iris fulva'' and the first syllable of Lamance (the common name of 'Iris foliosa' which was known at that time as ''Iris hexagona'' var. ''Lamancei''). Later, ''Iris foliosa'' was found to be a synonym of ''Iris brevicaulis''. The hybrids were found to be good garden plants and could flower more freely than either of the parents.<ref name=handbook/> Other crosses include with ''[[Iris giganticaerulea]]'' to produce 'Iris × vinicolor' Small and also with ''[[Iris savannarum]]'' to produce 'Iris × cacique' (J. Berry) N. C. Henderson.<ref name=efloras/>

''[[Iris brevicaulis]]'' and ''Iris fulva'' hybridize to produce [[Iris × fulvala]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Iris × fulvala Dykes {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77150705-1 |access-date=2025-04-29 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

Several American garden nurseries and plant breeders have created many Iris fulva cultivars including, 'Apricot Queen', 'August Flame', 'Autumn Fire', 'Baby Sis Pink' 'Bayou Bandit', 'Bayou Goula', 'Bazeti', 'Bolshevik', 'Bronze Red', 'Chocolate', 'Choctaw Tribe', 'Couperin', 'Cuprea', 'Devil's Advocate', 'Devil's Scion', 'Dwarf Terracotta', 'Dwarf Yellow', 'Edith Dupre', 'Encarnado', 'Esplanade', 'Flash', 'Fulvaflav', 'Fulvaflav', 'Fulva Special', 'Fulvaurea', 'Galloway-Lanoke', 'Georgia Peach', 'Golden Arrowhead', 'Gold In California', 'Gold Medallion', 'Gulf Sunshine', 'Karandash', 'Kraemer Tan', 'Kraemer Yellow', 'Le Vieux Carre', 'Louisiana Sunset', 'Margot Castellanos', 'Maringouin Freak', 'Maringouin Fulva', 'Marvell Gold', 'Mc Gregor', 'Red Fire', 'Sazerac', 'Slick Willie'.<ref name=american/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>

==Toxicity==
Some parts of the iris are poisonous.<ref name=tina/> Because both the foliage and rhizomes are deadly toxic, most mammalian herbivores usually leave iris untouched, although the [[muskrat]] (''Ondatra zibethicus'') occasionally feeds on their rhizomes and lower stems and the [[white-tailed deer]] (''Odocoileus virginianus'') sometimes nibbles the leaf edges.<ref name=illnois/>
